confirmed.title: A retried create (same ClientRowId) becomes a blind update with no version, silently overwriting edits made after the original create
confirmed.scenario: TargetOf (440-441) maps a create op whose ClientRowId already exists to that rug. UpdateAsync -> Merge then returns all incoming values unchanged because op.Version is null (597-598), so there is no three-way check. Verified: an Operator creates rug 9001 with origin 'aaa' (ClientRowId X). A merchant then edits origin to 'ccc' with the correct version (Saved). The Operator's original create op X is sent again: status Saved and the stored origin is back to 'aaa'. No conflict is reported. Real trigger: a create whose response was lost stays a rugId=null draft. After a reload the user (or a colleague) fixes the loaded row, then clicks «برگرداندن ردیف‌ها», which resends the stale create and reverts the fix. The same happens when switchDay leaves already-saved rows in the old day's draft key.
confirmed.fix: When a create op resolves to an existing rug by ClientRowId, do not apply values blindly. Either return the existing row as Saved without writing, or treat it as a stale edit: if the rug was updated after creation (UpdatedAt > CreatedAt / xmin moved), return Conflict with Current so the client merges. Alternatively, have the client keep the create's sent values as base so the three-way merge applies.

confirmed.title: Changing the intake day while rows are still unsaved can save day-A rows into day-B batches
confirmed.scenario: batchContext reads day.value at send time (line 61). switchDay (115-124) awaits ctrl.flush(), but flush returns immediately when a request is in flight (useGridSave.ts:204-207). When offline it just schedules another retry. switchDay then sets day.value to the new date before the old rows are replaced. If load() fails (offline) or is slower than the 1.5 s re-schedule, ctrl.rows still holds the old day's unsaved rows, and the retry/idle flush sends them with receivedAt = new day. Verified with a vitest probe: a row typed with day '2026-09-05' while saving failed (TypeError), then the day changed to '2026-09-06', and the retry request carried batch.receivedAt '2026-09-06' with serial 3778. The server (CreateAsync, plan.Day) then puts yesterday's rugs into today's (day, seller) batches: wrong intake day, wrong E7 footer and lump-cost group. drafts.schedule also writes the old rows under the new day's draft key.
confirmed.fix: Snapshot the day into each row (or into the request when the row is created) instead of reading day.value at send time. Or block the day switch until no rows are dirty or in flight, and replace or stop the controller's save timers before changing day.value, including when load() fails.

I could not refute it. At 82e2383 the code lets a day-A row that hasn't saved yet go out with day B's receivedAt. Nothing in the client or the server prevents this. The clearest case is offline or a 5xx error, which needs no race at all: the user types rows for day A, the save fails (TypeError or 5xx), and then the user picks day B.

Trace through IntakeGrid.island.vue switchDay (lines 115-124):
1. `ctrl.flushDrafts()` writes the draft under day A.
2. `await ctrl.flush()` runs useGridSave.flush. inFlight is false because the catch at useGridSave.ts:230 cleared it. collect() picks up the row, since saving was reset at line 227 and the row is still dirty. The send fails again, and scheduleRetry (lines 135-147) sets a retry timer that calls flush(). flush then returns.
3. `day.value = iso` runs at line 120. The retry timer and the idle timer are not stopped.
4. `await load()` fails offline (lines 80-85). It sets loadError and never calls ctrl.load, so ctrl.rows still holds day A's unsaved rows.

When the retry timer fires, flush calls buildRequest (useGridController.ts:249-255). That reads `options.batchContext()`, which is IntakeGrid line 61, `receivedAt: day.value`, so the value is now day B. Server side, RugGridService.cs:155 takes `day = request.Batch?.ReceivedAt`. CreateAsync (lines 507-513) then calls ResolveForDayAsync(plan.Day=B, seller), so day A's rugs go into the (day B, seller) batches. If a pending op only changes the seller of an existing rug, UpdateAsync (line 561) moves it to day B the same way.

Nothing guards against this. isReady and collect have no loading or day check, and switchDay never disposes or resets the save controller. While loadError is set, the template (`v-if="loadError"`) hides the DataGrid, and with it the retry countdown, so the user can't see the retries running. Retries keep going on the 2/4/8/16/30 s schedule. The rows are only cleared when the user presses "retry" (the load button) and that load succeeds. When the network comes back, the automatic retry will usually fire before that manual click, so the wrong-day save is the likely outcome.

The result is rugs stored under the wrong intake day and batch, which corrupts the per-day footer and the E7 lump-cost grouping.

confirmed.title: A row the server rejects is sent again every 1.5 s, forever
confirmed.scenario: collect() skips rows that are saving, in conflict or not ready, but not rows whose last result was Invalid. A 400/409/422 request error does not skip them either. After every flush, `if (again || collect().length > 0) schedule()` (line 260) queues another flush. Example: on the intake grid the user types a serial that is already used (or Delete clears a required size on a saved rug). The server answers 200 with status Invalid. The row keeps its dirty keys, so the identical op goes out again 1.5 s later, and keeps going until the user edits that cell. A probe test with a send that always returns Invalid counted 11 POSTs in 15 s. Each POST takes the tenant ledger advisory lock and runs a failed batch transaction plus a per-row retry. Each answer also resets row.nextFree and triggers lookupNextFree (one more GET /api/rugs/next-serial). The «شمارهٔ ۴۰۰۵ آزاد است [بله]» bar disappears and reappears under the user's finger, and the save status and row spinner flicker. A tab left open overnight sends tens of thousands of requests. With several rows, a whole-request 409 re-runs the isolate path each cycle (N+1 requests every 1.5 s).

For example, skip `row.status === 'invalid'` in collect(); markDirty already sets the status back to 'dirty' on the next edit. confirmed.title: Pasting a price, or typing it first in a new row, silently switches the purchase unit to «هر متر»
confirmed.scenario: paste() builds the plan with parseContext(null, null), so every money+unit cell is parsed with current = undefined. The basis then falls back to purchaseDefaultBasis (PerM2) and ignores the unit chip the target cell already has. Example in the rugs grid: a rug shows «کل ۴۰٬۰۰۰٬۰۰۰»; the user pastes 41000000 from Excel onto that cell. It is saved as {rate:41000000, basis:PerM2}, so the purchase cost becomes 41,000,000 × area (164,000,000 for a 2×2 rug). Typing the same number keeps «کل». In the intake grid, G.2 makes the price sticky for value and unit. Row 1 has «کل» (or «هر تخته»), and the user pastes 50 TSV rows that include a price column. materialize() copies the sticky unit, then the pasted cell overwrites it with PerM2, so every pasted row is billed per m². The same happens when the price is the first cell typed in the blank last row. commit() (line 576) parses with row.values[key] of the placeholder, which is undefined, and materialize() then skips that key. The unit chip changes quietly and the purchase totals are wrong by a factor equal to the area.
confirmed.fix: Parse each money+unit cell against the target cell's effective current value. In paste(), re-parse purchase cells per target row with current = row.values[key], or stickyValue(index, column) for the placeholder row. In commit(), use the sticky value when the row is the placeholder. Add tests for paste over a «کل» cell and paste under a «هر تخته» sticky row.

confirmed.title: Keyboard trap: neither Esc nor Tab can leave the grid until something has been undoable
confirmed.scenario: Tab and Shift+Tab never leave the grid. At the edges navTab returns null, the controller only bumps focusTick, and the key is preventDefault-ed. confirmed.title: Moving a column up in «ستون‌های جدول» drops keyboard focus to the page body
confirmed.scenario: move() swaps two keyed <li>s. For [A,B] → [B,A], Vue's keyed diff moves B's node before A with insertBefore. When the user activates B's «یکی جلوتر» button with the keyboard, the focused button is inside the moved node, so focus fixup sends it to <body> after every press. A keyboard user moving a column three places up must Tab back from the top of the page each time. This undercuts the WCAG 2.5.7 alternative the component provides.
confirmed.fix: After move(), on nextTick re-focus the same direction button of the moved column (look it up by column key).

votes.reason: The defect is real: focus is lost after "move up". In src/RugsManagment.Web/ClientApp/src/islands/settings/GridColumnsEditor.island.vue:76-82, move() swaps two neighbours in columns.value. The <li> elements are keyed (line 179, :key="column.key"), so Vue 3.5.39 (the version in package-lock.json) reorders them with patchKeyedChildren. When item i moves up, the longest-increasing-subsequence step keeps the other node in place and moves the earlier-in-new-order node. That is the clicked column's <li>, which contains the focused "یکی جلوتر" button (line 184-189). runtime-dom's nodeOps.insert is plain parent.insertBefore(child, anchor). It does not use moveBefore, so moving the subtree that holds the focused element resets document.activeElement to <body>. Nothing in the component puts focus back: there is no nextTick, no focus() and no template refs. "Move down" is not affected, because there Vue moves the other node. One part of the scenario is overstated. In Chromium the sequential-navigation start point survives, so the next Tab goes to the controls of the row after the swapped pair, not to the top of the page. The user still loses focus on every "up" press, cannot press Enter again to keep moving the column, and has to Shift+Tab back through the swapped row's controls (hide, two checkboxes, width field, name input, two arrows) to reach the button again. A screen-reader user is dropped to the document body. This is a low-severity accessibility defect, as reported.
votes.evidence: I checked this with a minimal Vue 3.5.39 copy of the same pattern: a keyed v-for over <li>, a swap-based move(index, delta), and the same :disabled bindings. Vue came from the commit's package-lock (npm ci in a throwaway snapshot), and the page was served on 127.0.0.1 and opened in the browser pane (Chromium). Steps and results: (1) I focused C's up button in [A,B,C,D] and pressed Enter. The order became [A,C,B,D] and document.activeElement was BODY. (2) I pressed Tab once and focus landed on D's up button, not C's and not the top of the page. (3) I focused A's down button and pressed Enter. The order became [C,A,B,D] and focus stayed on the same down button, so only moving up is affected. Relevant source: node_modules/@vue/runtime-dom/dist/runtime-dom.esm-bundler.js:27-28, "insert: (child, parent, anchor) => { parent.insertBefore(child, anchor || null) }", and grep found no moveBefore in runtime-dom or runtime-core. Component lines at 82e2383: :key="column.key" at 179, the up button's @click="move(index, -1)" at 189, and move() at 76-82 with no focus restore. The snapshot folder was deleted afterwards.

votes.reason: I could not refute this one. At 82e2383, move() in GridColumnsEditor.island.vue (lines 76-82) swaps two entries and assigns a new array. The rows are keyed by column.key (line 179), so Vue 3.5.39 (the locked version) uses its keyed-children diff to apply the swap. When a column moves up, the diff physically moves the node of the column you pressed, inserting it before its neighbour with insertBefore. The neighbour's node is the one it keeps in place. Moving a node that holds the focused button sends focus to <body>. Nothing in the component puts focus back: there is no nextTick, no focus() call, no ref. Moving a column down keeps focus, because the other row's node is the one moved. I reproduced the up case in Chromium with a minimal Vue 3.5.39 page that uses the same structure (keyed li rows, the same move() swap, the same disabled rules). The finding's claim about where the next Tab lands is also true in Chromium.
votes.evidence:
Code at 82e2383, src/RugsManagment.Web/ClientApp/src/islands/settings/GridColumnsEditor.island.vue:

Repro in Chromium (browser pane), with Vue 3.5.39 from jsdelivr and the same template shape. I focused each button, clicked it, then checked after Vue.nextTick:
- "up" on D, order A,B,C,D: activeElement was BODY, new order A,B,D,C, and the button node was the same element, just moved.
- "down" on A: activeElement stayed on down-A (focus kept).
- "up" on C: activeElement was BODY.

Impact: a keyboard or screen-reader user who presses the up button on any column below position 2 loses focus after every press. (Moving the second column to the top would also leave its up button disabled, which drops focus too.) A keyboard user cannot easily repeat the move, which weakens the non-drag alternative the component exists to provide (WCAG 2.5.7). Severity is low: this is about accessibility, and no data is affected. The temporary repro files were deleted.

unverified.title: Bale numbers and line Seq are picked before the tenant lock, and the deferred unique constraint only fails at COMMIT, where nothing translates the error (HTTP 500, whole lines batch lost)
unverified.scenario: TargetBaleAsync (LineService.cs:393-404) runs FindBaleByNumberTrackedAsync, and BaleService.CreateAsync (BaleService.cs:72) runs MaxBaleNumberAsync+1. Both happen before the ledger advisory lock, which is only taken inside SaveChanges. The constraint UX_Bales_Shipment_Number is DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED (migration 20261004194543_Shipments.cs:123-126). So when two requests create the same bale number, the second INSERT succeeds and the 23505 is raised at COMMIT (LedgerPass.cs:80 or UnitOfWork.cs:49). LedgerSession.cs:192 maps 23505 only during flush, and ApiExceptionFilter has no PostgresException branch, so the request returns an unhandled 500. Reproduced on a throwaway DB at 82e2383. (1) 10 parallel POST /api/shipments/{id}/bales with no number: 8 returned 500 'PostgresException 23505 UX_Bales_Shipment_Number'; only bales 1 and 2 were created. (2) 8 Operators each sent lines/batch [{op:'add', baleNumber:5, rugId:own}] at once (two phones pressing «نگلهٔ بعد», then scanning): 4 requests got 500 and their whole batch was rolled back. 3 of the 4 that succeeded got the same Seq 2 in bale 5, because PlaceAsync (LineService.cs:421-424) also reads max Seq before the lock.
unverified.fix: Take ILedgerLock.AcquireAsync inside the transaction before reading or allocating bale numbers and Seq: in LineService.BatchAsync before the op loop, and in BaleService.CreateAsync/UpdateAsync wrapped in ExecuteInTransactionAsync. Also translate a commit-time PostgresException 23505 into DuplicateKeyException (409), in OwnedTransaction.CommitAsync and UnitOfWork.ExecuteInTransactionAsync. Alternatively, run SET CONSTRAINTS "UX_Bales_Shipment_Number" IMMEDIATE for every save except Renumber.

rejected.title: Decimal overflow and huge round() digit counts crash composition after the layout passed validation
rejected.why: At 82e2383 the claimed failure (preview, print and xlsx returning 500 for a saved template) cannot happen, because the document engine has no production caller and nobody can author a template. The underlying library behaviour is accurate but only latent. If Evaluator.Round gets a huge digits argument, `(int)Math.Truncate(digits)` at Evaluator.cs:227 throws OverflowException, since decimal-to-int conversion is always checked. A decimal product above about 7.9e28 at line 160 also throws, and neither LayoutValidator nor DocumentComposer catches these. Reaching that code at this commit is not possible: 1) DocumentComposer.Compose and LayoutValidator.Validate are called only from tests. `git grep` across src finds no Web file that references Features.Documents. 2) The Application AddDocumentsModule body is `services => services`. 3) There is no DocumentTemplate entity, no template repository, no DocumentTemplateSeedContributor, and no documents or templates controller. "POST /documents/rugs.xlsx" appears only in a doc comment. 4) Per the briefs, the composer is first wired to preview, print and xlsx in P6-wiring (p6w-brief.md: DocumentsApiController, DocumentsController, read-only template endpoints). Template writes and validate-expression come later still, in P7 (p7-brief.md), behind the Configure policy. 5) Only the configurator, a privileged user, could ever reach it, and only by typing absurd constants. Real data cannot overflow: the largest realistic product, USD total times the rial rate, is about 2e10, against decimal's limit of about 7.9e28. So the issue is a hardening item for P7's validate-expression and template-save path, not a defect at this commit. | The arithmetic part is correct: in Evaluator.cs:160, multiplying two decimals throws OverflowException when the result passes about 7.9e28, and at line 227 `(int)Math.Truncate(digits)` throws for digits such as 1e10. But the reported failure cannot happen at 82e2383. Nothing outside the engine calls DocumentComposer: there is no preview, print or xlsx endpoint, no DocumentTemplate entity or table, and no designer or API that lets a user save a custom layout. The P6 brief says this package is pure: "no entities, no DB, no web (P6-wiring does those after P4a+P5)". The only layouts are the two embedded defaults. Their expressions are `round(col.length*col.width,2)` and `round(col.area*col.rate,2)`, with a literal 2 for the digits and rug-scale values, so neither overflow can occur. The spec's E.2 LayoutValidator rules also do not require numeric-range or round-digit bounds, so the validator is not breaking a stated rule. This is at most a hardening item for the future P6-wiring/P7 designer, not a defect reachable at this commit.

rejected.title: GET /api/grid/intake answers 200 with an empty grid for another tenant's batchId instead of 404
rejected.why: The described behaviour does happen, but it is not a defect. On GET /api/grid/intake, `batchId` is a query filter scoped to the tenant, not a resource the request acts on. Under the code at 82e2383 a foreign batch id gets exactly the same 200-with-empty-rows response as a made-up GUID, or as one of the tenant's own batches from a different day. So nothing leaks, there is no way to probe whether an id exists, and there are no side effects. The 404 rule exists to block those leaks and probes, and none is possible here. The existing filter in the codebase already works this way: /api/rugs?batchId= is also a tenant-scoped filter that returns an empty page for a foreign id. The spec's GET grid contract asks for a 404 only for an unknown gridId. The spec's isolation test works from route values, and the only route value on this action is gridId. Comparing this with POST /api/grid/rugs/batch does not hold up. That endpoint writes rugs into the batch it is given, so it must check ownership before writing. The GET only narrows a read that is already restricted to the tenant. | The reported behaviour does happen, but it is not a tenant-isolation defect. A foreign batchId gets 200 with an empty grid, and a random Guid that matches no batch gets exactly the same response. So nothing leaks: no rows, totals or existence oracle, and no side effects. In this GET, batchId is only a list filter, the same as /api/rugs?batchId= and the `rugs` grid's RugQuery.BatchId, which also return empty and never 404 for a foreign id. The "unknown id -> 404" in the spec's grid row refers to the gridId that picks the IGridSource. The 404 rule for cross-tenant ids covers accessing or writing a tenant-owned entity. The one path that writes into a batch, POST /api/grid/rugs/batch, does reject a foreign batch with 404.

rejected.title: Rugs grid: restoring a draft for a rug not on the first page shifts the paging offset, so one rug never loads
rejected.why:
The finding assumes the server starts each page at row `skip`. It does not. RugsGridSource.LoadAsync turns `skip` into a page number: `var take = Math.Clamp(request.Take ?? DefaultTake, 5, RugQuery.MaxPageSize)` (MaxPageSize = 100), then `Page = skip / take + 1` (RugsGridSource.cs:73-75). RugRepository then does `.Skip((query.Page - 1) * query.PageSize)` (RugRepository.cs:125). So any skip from S to S+99 returns the page that starts at S.

The client always holds a full prefix of server rows, S (a multiple of 100), plus E restored draft rows outside that prefix. While E is under 100, `skip = S + E` still maps to the next correct page. When that page arrives, `append()` drops the server copy of any restored rug in it (useGridController.ts:384-391), so E shrinks and the count corrects itself.

Worked example with the real page size: page 1 loads 100 rows, and restoring an off-page draft makes rows.length 101. loadMore sends skip=101, which becomes page 101/100+1 = 2, i.e. rows 100-199. The finding's own numbers give the same result: skip=201 maps to page 3, which starts at row 200. Row 200 is loaded, so no rug is skipped.

The secondary claim (a restored row shows only its dirty keys) is also not lasting. `restoreDrafts()` calls `save.flushSoon()`. On a Saved result, `applyOpResult` copies the server's `result.current` into the row, and GridDtos.cs:126 documents `current` as every cell's current server value. It also sets sku, so the row fills in once the save goes through. | The finding assumes the server applies skip as an exact row offset, and it does not. RugsGridSource.LoadAsync turns skip into a page number by integer division, Page = skip / take + 1, and take is clamped to 100. RugRepository then uses the offset (Page-1)*PageSize, so any skip that is not on a page boundary is rounded down to the start of that page. With one restored draft from page 2, the client sends skip=101 (the clamp makes the real page 100 rows, not 200) or skip=201 in the reviewer's numbers. The server still returns the whole page that starts at the boundary, so the rug the reviewer says is lost is returned. append() then drops only the rows already present by rugId, which is the draft's own rug, and the count lines up again after that page arrives. The "only dirty keys" display is also brief: restoreDrafts calls save.flushSoon(), and a Saved result carries current = Builder.Values(saved), which applyOpResult copies into the cells that are not dirty.
